subChunks.title: Events vs Commands, Event Sourcing & Choreography vs Orchestration
subChunks.hookHtml: Event-driven architecture fundamentally changes how services communicate — from 'tell me what to do' (commands) to 'here's what happened' (events). This shift has profound implications for coupling, scalability, and auditability. It's also where some of the deepest architectural decisions of your career will be made.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Events vs Commands

Commands: tell a service to do something. Directed — sent to a specific target. The sender knows the receiver. Example: SendEmail, ChargeCard, CreateShipment. Implies intent and expectation of outcome.

Events: record that something happened. Broadcast — published to a topic; any service may listen. The publisher does not know who listens. Example: OrderPlaced, PaymentFailed, SpellCast. Describes a fact about the past.

Events decouple producers from consumers. Adding a new reaction to OrderPlaced (e.g. loyalty points) requires no changes to the order service — just add a new subscriber.

Event Sourcing

Instead of storing current state, store the sequence of events that led to that state. Reconstruct current state by replaying events.

// Traditional: store current balance
Account { balance: 850 }

// Event sourced: store events
[AccountOpened(1000), Withdrawal(200), Deposit(100), Withdrawal(50)]
// Replay: 1000 - 200 + 100 - 50 = 850

Benefits: full audit trail, temporal queries (state at any point in time), event replay for debugging or new projections. Costs: eventual consistency of read models, projection maintenance, storage growth.

Choreography vs Orchestration

Choreography: each service knows what events to react to and what events to emit. No central coordinator. Services are fully decoupled but the overall flow is distributed — hard to visualise or debug.

Orchestration: a central orchestrator (saga orchestrator, workflow engine) tells each service what to do and handles the overall flow. Easier to understand and monitor; central point of failure; tighter coupling to the orchestrator.

// Choreography: Order → emits OrderPlaced
//   Inventory reacts → emits InventoryReserved
//   Payment reacts  → emits PaymentCharged
//   Shipping reacts → emits ShipmentCreated
// No central coordinator. Each service independently reacts.

// Orchestration: OrderSaga coordinates
class OrderSaga {
    void handleOrderCreated(OrderCreated event) {
        inventoryService.reserve(event.items);
        paymentService.charge(event.total);
        shippingService.createShipment(event.address);
    }
}

storyBeats.text: The old Academy system called services directly: place-order called reserve-inventory called charge-payment called create-shipment. Adding loyalty points required modifying order placement. Changing the payment provider required updating inventory. Every change rippled everywhere. The new design emits events. Each service does its job and announces what happened. New features subscribe without touching existing code.

storyBeats.speaker: Architecture Lead Mira
storyBeats.text: The key insight of event-driven design is that events describe facts. OrderPlaced is immutable truth — it happened. Anyone who needs to know can subscribe. The order service does not call inventory, does not call payment, does not know either exists. That is genuine decoupling.

storyBeats.speaker: Architecture Lead Mira
storyBeats.text: Choreography versus orchestration is not a religion. Both work. Choreography gives you maximum decoupling but makes the overall flow invisible — it lives in no single place. Orchestration makes the flow explicit and auditable but re-couples services to the orchestrator. For complex, long-running business processes I often lean toward orchestration just so I can visualise what state the process is in.

storyBeats.speaker: Event sourcing — account projection
Architecture Lead Mira
storyBeats.text: Event sourcing is powerful but the cost is real. Your read models are projections — rebuilt from events — which means eventual consistency. And every schema change to an event type is a migration challenge because old events are immutable. Use event sourcing where auditability and temporal queries are requirements, not as a default.

learningObjectives: Distinguish events from commands and explain the decoupling benefit of event-driven design
Explain event sourcing: how state is reconstructed from an event stream and the trade-offs vs state persistence
Compare choreography and orchestration patterns and identify when each is more appropriate
Implement a simple in-memory event bus in Java supporting event type routing to handlers
commonMistakes: Publishing commands disguised as events (e.g. 'PleaseChargeCard') — events describe what happened, not what should happen
Using event sourcing everywhere as a default — it adds significant complexity and is only justified for specific requirements
Choosing choreography for complex flows without tooling to visualise the overall saga state
Making events mutable or versioning them carelessly — event store consumers break on schema changes
assessmentCriteria: Can write an event definition and explain why it describes a past fact, not a future action
Can trace the steps of an order-placed saga in both choreography and orchestration styles
Can implement event sourcing for a simple aggregate (e.g. bank account) with replay
Can explain what a projection is and why event sourcing produces eventually consistent read models
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain event-driven architecture to a developer who only knows REST APIs. What is the difference between a command and an event? Why does emitting events reduce coupling? What do you lose in the trade?
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Write an EventBus class that routes events by type to registered handlers:

  1. Use Map<Class<?>, List<Consumer<Object>>> handlers
  2. Method <T> void subscribe(Class<T> type, Consumer<T> handler) — store the handler
  3. Method void publish(Object event) — look up handlers by event's runtime class and call each (cast with Class.cast)
  4. Define two simple record event types: SpellCast(String name, int damage) and MageLoggedIn(String username)
  5. In main: subscribe to SpellCast (print 'Spell fired: name') and MageLoggedIn (print 'Mage arrived: username'). Publish one of each.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Implement simple event sourcing for a SpellBook aggregate. Define sealed interface SpellEvent with records SpellAdded(String name, int damage) and SpellRemoved(String name). Write class SpellBook with a List<SpellEvent> eventLog. Methods: void addSpell(String name, int damage) and void removeSpell(String name) both append to the log. Method Map<String, Integer> currentState() replays the event log from scratch to build and return the current spell registry. In main: add Fireball(300), add Frost(150), remove Fireball. Print currentState — should show only Frost:150.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the difference between an event and a command in event-driven architecture?
options: Events are synchronous; commands are asynchronous
Events describe something that happened (fact); commands tell a service to do something (intent)
Events are stored; commands are not
Events are published to queues; commands are published to topics
questions.answer: Events describe something that happened (fact); commands tell a service to do something (intent)
questions.explanation: An event is an immutable record of something that occurred: OrderPlaced, PaymentFailed. It does not mandate any reaction. A command directs a specific action: PlaceOrder, ChargeCard. Events decouple producers from consumers because the publisher does not know or care who reacts — any number of subscribers can independently handle the same event.

questions.prompt: In event sourcing, how is the current state of an entity (e.g. account balance) obtained?
options: Read the current_balance column from the accounts table
Query the most recent event in the event log
Replay all events in order from the beginning of the event stream
questions.answer: Replay all events in order from the beginning of the event stream
questions.explanation: Event sourcing stores the sequence of events, not the current state. To get the current state, you replay all events through an event handler function that produces the final state. Snapshotting (storing state at a checkpoint) is used to avoid replaying from the beginning in large event streams — you replay only from the latest snapshot.

questions.prompt: A complex order fulfilment flow involves inventory, payment, and shipping. A bug causes the flow to get stuck midway. Which pattern makes it easiest to inspect the current state of the flow and determine where it is stuck?
options: Choreography — each service independently emits events
Orchestration — a central saga orchestrator tracks the flow state explicitly
Pub/sub — the topic history shows all events
questions.answer: Orchestration — a central saga orchestrator tracks the flow state explicitly
questions.explanation: With choreography, the overall flow state is distributed across multiple services' event logs — reconstructing it requires correlating events across systems. With orchestration, the saga orchestrator holds the explicit state of each in-flight process. When something is stuck, you query the orchestrator's state store and immediately see which step failed and what compensating action is needed.
